statement: Let $\{f_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a smooth family of positive [densities](c:probability-density-function) on one open interval $S$. If for some $n>k$ the $n$-sample has a smooth [sufficient statistic](c:sufficient-statistic) with values in $\mathbb R^k$, then the family is an [exponential family](c:exponential-family): $f_\theta(x)=h(x)\exp\bigl(\sum_{j\le r}\eta_j(\theta)T_j(x)-A(\theta)\bigr)$ with $r\le k$.

hypotheses.text: The [densities](c:probability-density-function) $f_\theta$ are positive on one open interval $S$ and smooth in $(x,\theta)$.
The parameter set $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open and connected.

For some $n>k$, the map $T\colon S^n\to\mathbb R^k$ is a smooth [sufficient statistic](c:sufficient-statistic): $\prod_{i\le n}f_\theta(x_i)=g(T(x),\theta)\,h_0(x)$ with $T$ and $g$ of class $C^1$ and $h_0>0$.

conclusion: There are $r\le k$ functions $T_j$ on $S$, functions $\eta_j$ on $\Theta$, and functions $h>0$ and $A$ with $f_\theta(x)=h(x)\exp\bigl(\sum_{j\le r}\eta_j(\theta)T_j(x)-A(\theta)\bigr)$.

proofs.name: Finite-rank kernel
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the factored likelihood in $\theta$ and in the observations, show that the mixed derivative of $\log f$ has rank at most $k$, and integrate back.
proofs.scope: The smooth case with fixed support, as treated by Darmois, Koopman and Pitman. The case $n\le k$ is excluded, because then $T(x)=x$ is always sufficient.

roles.why: Positivity makes $\log f_\theta$ smooth, and the interval $S$ lets $x$-derivatives be integrated back.
A connected $\Theta$ makes a function with zero $\theta$-gradient constant in $\theta$.
The factorization through $T$ puts the derivative vectors in a space of dimension at most $k$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the logarithm of the factored likelihood in the parameter.
steps.detail: Put $\ell(x,\theta)=\log f_\theta(x)$. The factorization gives $\sum_{i\le n}\ell(x_i,\theta)=\log g(T(x),\theta)+\log h_0(x)$. Differentiating in $\theta_a$ removes $h_0$: $\sum_i\partial_{\theta_a}\ell(x_i,\theta)=G_a(T(x),\theta)$ with $G_a=\partial_{\theta_a}\log g$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate in each observation to confine the derivative vectors to a fixed $k$-dimensional space.
steps.detail: Differentiating in $x_i$ gives $\partial_x\partial_{\theta_a}\ell(x_i,\theta)=\sum_{j\le k}\partial_{T_j}G_a(T(x),\theta)\,\partial_{x_i}T_j(x)$. So the vector $v_{a,\theta}=\bigl(\partial_x\partial_{\theta_a}\ell(x_i,\theta)\bigr)_{i\le n}$ lies in the span of the $k$ columns of $DT(x)$. This span does not depend on $(a,\theta)$.

steps.slogan: Show that every $(k+1)\times(k+1)$ minor of the kernel $K=\partial_x\partial_{\theta_a}\ell$ vanishes.
steps.detail: Take points $x_1,\dots,x_n\in S$ and $k+1$ pairs $s_l=(a_l,\theta_l)$. The vectors $v_{s_l}\in\mathbb R^n$ lie in a space of dimension at most $k$, so the matrix $[K(x_i;s_l)]$ has rank at most $k$. Hence all its $(k+1)\times(k+1)$ minors vanish.

steps.slogan: Write the kernel as at most $k$ products of a function of $x$ and a function of $(a,\theta)$.
steps.detail: Let $r\le k$ be the largest rank of a matrix $[K(x_i;s_l)]$, and fix $x_1,\dots,x_r$ and $s_1,\dots,s_r$ with a nonzero minor $M$. Vanishing of the $(r+1)$-minors gives $K(x;s)=\sum_{i,l}K(x;s_l)(M^{-1})_{li}K(x_i;s)$. So $K=\sum_{j\le r}U_j(x)W_j(s)$ with independent $U_j$ and independent $W_j$.

steps.slogan: Integrate in $x$ and in $\theta$, then exponentiate to read off the exponential form.
steps.detail:
Let $T_j(x)=\int_{x_0}^xU_j$ and $D=\ell-\ell(x_0,\cdot)$. Then $
abla_	heta D=\sum_jT_jW_j$. The $T_j$ are independent, so each $W_j$ is a combination of values $
abla_	heta D(x^i,\cdot)$ and equals $
abla\eta_j$. Then $D-\sum_jT_j\eta_j$ depends on $x$ only, so $\ell=\sum_j\eta_jT_j+a(x)+b(	heta)$. Here $b=\ell(x_0,\cdot)$. Take $h=e^{a}$ and $A=-b$.

concepts.c:probability-density-function: Positive smooth densities give a smooth logarithm $\ell$ of the likelihood.
concepts.c:sufficient-statistic: Factorization through $T$ forces the rank bound on the mixed derivative.
concepts.c:exponential-family: The integrated form of the log-density is the definition of an exponential family.

source.note: The classical differentiable argument of Darmois (1935), Koopman (Trans. AMS 39 (1936), 399-409) and Pitman (1936), written as a finite-rank kernel argument.

statement: Let $\mu$ be a complex [measure](c:measure) on the circle $\mathbb T$ whose [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) $\hat\mu(n)=\int e^{-int}\,d\mu(t)$ vanish for all $n<0$. Then $\mu$ is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $m=dt/2\pi$: $d\mu=f\,dm$ with $f\in L^1(m)$ in the [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) $H^1$.

hypotheses.text: $\mu$ is a complex Borel [measure](c:measure) of finite total variation on $\mathbb T$.
The [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) satisfy $\hat\mu(n)=0$ for every $n<0$.

conclusion: There is $f\in L^1(m)$ with $d\mu=f\,dm$ and $\hat f(n)=0$ for every $n<0$.

proofs.name: Poisson extension and $H^1$
proofs.slogan: Extend $\mu$ to a holomorphic function in the disc, show that it lies in $H^1$, and identify the boundary density.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for complex $\mu$. The proof quotes the boundary theory of $H^1$ (Riesz factorization).

roles.why: A finite measure has bounded Fourier coefficients and a Poisson integral with bounded integral means.
Only nonnegative frequencies occur, so the Poisson integral is a holomorphic power series.

steps.slogan: Extend $\mu$ to a function $F$ holomorphic in the unit disc.
steps.detail: Put $F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}\hat\mu(n)z^n$. Since $|\hat\mu(n)|\le\|\mu\|$, the series converges for $|z|<1$ and $F$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function). Because $\hat\mu(n)=0$ for $n<0$, $F(re^{i\theta})=\int P_r(\theta-t)\,d\mu(t)$, the Poisson integral of $\mu$ with kernel $P_r(s)=\sum_nr^{|n|}e^{ins}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integral means of $F$ by the total variation of $\mu$.
steps.detail: The [Poisson kernel](c:poisson-kernel) is positive with $\int P_r\,dm=1$. Fubini gives $\int|F(re^{i\theta})|\,dm(\theta)\le\iint P_r(\theta-t)\,dm(\theta)\,d|\mu|(t)=\|\mu\|$ for every $r<1$. So $F$ lies in the [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) $H^1$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the boundary function $f$ of $F$ and the $L^1$ limit of $F_r$.
steps.detail: The Riesz factorization $F=G\,H$ with $G,H\in H^2$ and the boundary theory of $H^2$ show that $F_r(\theta)=F(re^{i\theta})$ converges almost everywhere and in $L^1(m)$ to some $f\in L^1(m)$. This is the boundary behaviour of $H^1$ (Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapter 17).

steps.slogan: Compare the Fourier coefficients of $f$ and $\mu$.
steps.detail: $L^1$ convergence gives $\hat f(n)=\lim_{r\to1}\hat F_r(n)$. Here $\hat F_r(n)=r^n\hat\mu(n)$ for $n\ge0$ and $\hat F_r(n)=0$ for $n<0$. So $\hat f(n)=\hat\mu(n)$ for every $n$, because $\hat\mu(n)=0$ for $n<0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\mu=f\,dm$ because Fourier coefficients determine a measure.
steps.detail: The measures $\mu$ and $f\,dm$ have the same Fourier coefficients. Trigonometric polynomials are dense in $C(\mathbb T)$, so $\int\phi\,d\mu=\int\phi f\,dm$ for every continuous $\phi$. The uniqueness in the Riesz representation theorem gives $\mu=f\,dm$.

concepts.c:measure: A finite complex measure has Fourier coefficients and a Poisson integral.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: Vanishing negative coefficients give holomorphy; matching coefficients identify $\mu$.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Lebesgue measure is the reference measure for the density $f$.
concepts.c:hardy-space: Membership of $F$ in $H^1$ gives boundary values in $L^1$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The Poisson integral becomes a holomorphic power series in the disc.
concepts.c:poisson-kernel: Positivity and unit mass of the kernel bound the integral means.

source.note: The classical proof through $H^1$, as in Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapter 17 (the F. and M. Riesz theorem).

statement: Let $(M,[g])$ be a [conformal manifold](c:conformal-manifold) of dimension $n\ge3$ with metric bundle $\mathcal G$. An ambient metric $\tilde g$ exists near $\mathcal G\times\{0\}$: it is homogeneous of degree 2 and tautological on $\mathcal G$, and its [Ricci tensor](c:ricci-curvature) is $O(\rho^\infty)$ for odd $n$ and $O(\rho^{n/2-1})$ for even $n$. It is unique up to diffeomorphism and that order.

hypotheses.text: $(M,[g])$ is a [conformal manifold](c:conformal-manifold) with metric bundle $\mathcal G$.
The dimension satisfies $n\ge3$.

conclusion: A homogeneous ambient metric with the stated Ricci order exists and is unique up to diffeomorphism and up to that order.

proofs.name: Formal expansion in $\rho$
proofs.slogan: Put the ambient metric in normal form, solve the Ricci-flat equation order by order in $\rho$, and sum the series with Borel's lemma.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline of the formal theory (Taylor series in $\rho$), made smooth by Borel's lemma. Its [Einstein](c:einstein-metric) counterpart in dimension $n+1$ is the [Poincaré metric](c:poincare-metric), which the book treats in chapter 4.

roles.why: The conformal class gives the metric bundle, the dilations and the choice of a representative $g$.
The order-by-order analysis and its indicial factor are written for $n\ge3$.

steps.slogan: Reduce any ambient metric to a normal form relative to a chosen representative $g$.
steps.detail: Choose $g\in[g]$ and coordinates $(t,x,\rho)$. Homogeneity and the condition that the $\rho$-lines are geodesics give a diffeomorphism that brings $\tilde g$ to $2\rho\,dt^2+2t\,dt\,d\rho+t^2g_\rho$, where $g_\rho$ is a family of metrics on $M$ with $g_0=g$ (Fefferman and Graham, chapter 2).

steps.slogan: Write the Ricci-flat condition on $g_\rho$ as a singular ordinary differential equation in $\rho$.
steps.detail: In normal form $\mathrm{Ric}(\tilde g)=0$ becomes a system for $g_\rho$. Its leading part is $\rho\,g_\rho''-(\tfrac n2-1)g_\rho'-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(g_\rho^{-1}g_\rho')\,g_\rho$, and the [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) of $g_\rho$ is a source term. The equation is singular at $\rho=0$ (chapter 3).

steps.slogan: Solve for the Taylor coefficients of $g_\rho$ one order at a time.
steps.detail: Differentiating the equation $k-1$ times at $\rho=0$ shows that $\partial_\rho^kg$ enters with the factor $k-\tfrac n2$ in its trace-free part. The other components of the equation fix the trace. So $\partial_\rho^kg$ is determined by lower orders for $k<n/2$, and for every $k$ when $n$ is odd.

steps.slogan: Locate the obstruction at order $\rho^{n/2}$ when $n$ is even.
steps.detail: For even $n$ the factor vanishes at $k=n/2$. The trace-free part of the equation then has a solution only if a tensor built from lower-order data vanishes. This tensor is the obstruction tensor (the Bach tensor for $n=4$). So $\mathrm{Ric}(\tilde g)=O(\rho^{n/2-1})$ is the best order, and the trace-free part of $\partial_\rho^{n/2}g$ stays free.

steps.slogan: Sum the Taylor series by Borel's lemma and check uniqueness up to diffeomorphism.
steps.detail: Borel's lemma gives a smooth family $g_\rho$ with the computed Taylor series. Two ambient metrics in normal form have the same coefficients up to the stated order, so the diffeomorphism of the first step identifies them to that order. The result does not depend on the choice of $g\in[g]$.

concepts.c:conformal-manifold: The conformal class defines the metric bundle on which the ambient metric lives.
concepts.c:ricci-curvature: The ambient condition is Ricci flatness, solved to a finite or infinite order.
concepts.c:einstein-metric: Ricci-flat ambient metrics are the Einstein metrics of the construction.
concepts.c:poincare-metric: The Poincaré metric is the equivalent Einstein form in dimension $n+1$.

source.ref: C. Fefferman and C. R. Graham, The Ambient Metric, Annals of Mathematics Studies 178, Princeton University Press, 2012 (Theorem 2.9; chapters 2 and 3)
source.note: The outline follows the formal theory of chapters 2 and 3: normal form, the equation in $\rho$, the indicial factor, the obstruction tensor and uniqueness.

statement: Let $\mu$ be a [measure](c:measure) on $\mathbb R$, $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $I$ the closed interval with ends $a,b$ and $J$ the same interval without its left end. If $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $I$, $g$ is $\mu$-integrable on $a..b$ and $g\ge0$ $\mu$-a.e. on $J$, then $\int_a^bfg\,d\mu=f(c)\int_a^bg\,d\mu$ for some $c\in I$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed interval $I$.
The function $g$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) for $\mu$ on $a..b$.
$g(x)\ge0$ for $\mu$-almost every $x\in J$.

proofs.name: Reduction to a connected set
proofs.slogan: Turn the interval integral into an integral over the connected set $(a,b]$ and use the set-integral mean value theorem.
proofs.scope: All $a,b$: the case $a=b$ is trivial and $a>b$ is reduced to $a<b$ by swapping the ends. The interval integral is $\int_{(a,b]}$ for $a<b$.

roles.why: Continuity makes $f$ bounded on $I$ and continuous on the connected set $(a,b]$.
Integrability of $g$ gives integrability of $fg$ and of $g$ on $(a,b]$.
Almost everywhere nonnegativity is the sign condition of the set-integral version.

steps.slogan: Dispose of the case $a=b$ and reduce to $a<b$.
steps.detail: If $a=b$, both sides are $0$ and $c=a$ works. If $a>b$, swap the ends: $I$ and $J$ do not change, and both sides of the identity change sign. So assume $a<b$.

steps.slogan: Replace the interval integral by an integral over the [connected](c:connected-space) set $s=(a,b]$.
steps.detail: For $a<b$, $\int_a^bh\,d\mu=\int_{s}h\,d\mu$ for every integrable $h$. The set $s$ is an interval, hence connected and measurable, and $s\subseteq I$.

steps.slogan: Show that $fg$ is integrable on $s$.
steps.detail: A continuous function on the compact interval $I$ is bounded and measurable. So $|fg|\le\sup_I|f|\cdot|g|$, and $fg$ is integrable on $s$ because $g$ is.

steps.slogan: Cite the set-integral version for $s$ with the same $f$, $g$ and $\mu$.
steps.detail: The set $s$ is connected and measurable, $f$ is continuous on $s$, and $g$ and $fg$ are integrable on $s$ with $g\ge0$ a.e. on $s$. The set-integral version gives $c\in s$ with $\int_sfg\,d\mu=f(c)\int_sg\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Translate back to interval integrals and place $c$ in $I$.
steps.detail: Rewrite $\int_s$ as $\int_a^b$ on both sides. The point $c$ lies in $s\subseteq I$, so $\int_a^bfg\,d\mu=f(c)\int_a^bg\,d\mu$ with $c\in I$.

concepts.c:measure: The measure may be any measure on the line, not only Lebesgue measure.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity gives boundedness of $f$ and the intermediate value property on $s$.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability of $g$ makes both integrals finite and gives integrability of $fg$.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness of $(a,b]$ is what the set-integral version needs.

source.note: mathlib treats a=b, swaps to a<b, takes s = uIoc a b (isConnected_Ioc, uIoc_subset_uIcc), shows integrability of f*g (IntervalIntegrable.continuousOn_smul) and applies exists_eq_const_mul_setIntegral_of_ae_nonneg.

statement: Let $s$ be a [connected](c:connected-space) [measurable set](c:measurable-set) in a topological measure space $(\alpha,\mu)$. If $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $s$, $g$ and $fg$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $s$, and $g\ge0$ on $s$, then $\int_sfg\,d\mu=f(c)\int_sg\,d\mu$ for some $c\in s$.

hypotheses.text: The set $s$ is [connected](c:connected-space) and [measurable](c:measurable-set).
The function $f\colon\alpha\to\mathbb R$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $s$.
The functions $g$ and $fg$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $s$ for $\mu$.
$g(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in s$.

proofs.name: Density measure and average
proofs.slogan: Weight $\mu$ by $g$, then use that a continuous function on a connected set takes the average value of a measure on that set.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; pointwise nonnegativity is used only through its almost everywhere form. A connected set is nonempty by definition, which the degenerate case needs.

roles.why: Connectedness gives the intermediate value step, and measurability makes $\nu(s)$ and the restricted integrals meaningful.
Continuity of $f$ on $s$ is what the intermediate value property needs.
Integrability makes $\nu(s)$ finite and $f$ integrable for $\nu$.
Nonnegativity of $g$ makes $\nu$ a measure.

steps.slogan: Weaken $g\ge0$ on $s$ to $g\ge0$ almost everywhere for $\mu$ restricted to $s$.
steps.detail: A property that holds at every point of the measurable set $s$ holds almost everywhere for the restriction of $\mu$ to $s$. This is the only sign information that the rest of the proof uses.

steps.slogan: Define the measure $\nu$ with density $g$ and rewrite both integrals as $\nu$-integrals.
steps.detail:
Let $
u(A)=\int_Ag\,d\mu$ for measurable $A\subseteq s$. Almost everywhere nonnegativity makes $
u$ a measure. Then $\int_sfg\,d\mu=\int_sf\,d
u$ and $\int_sg\,d\mu=
u(s)<\infty$, and $f$ is $
u$-integrable because $fg$ is $\mu$-integrable.

steps.slogan: Treat the case $\nu(s)=0$ separately.
steps.detail: If $\nu(s)=0$, then $g=0$ almost everywhere on $s$, so $fg=0$ almost everywhere and both sides of the identity are $0$. Any $c\in s$ works, because $s$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: For $\nu(s)>0$, find points where $f$ is below and above its $\nu$-average.
steps.detail:
Let $m=
u(s)^{-1}\int_sf\,d
u$. If $f>m$ at every point of $s$, then $\int_s(f-m)\,d
u>0$, which is false. So the set $\{f\le m\}$ is nonempty, and in the same way $\{f\ge m\}$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Join the two points through the connected set to find $c$ with $f(c)=m$.
steps.detail: Since $f$ is continuous on the connected set $s$, the image $f(s)$ is an interval. It contains a value $\le m$ and a value $\ge m$, so it contains $m$. Hence $f(c)=m$ for some $c\in s$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the average equation by $\nu(s)$ to obtain the identity.
steps.detail: By the density step, $\int_sfg\,d\mu=\int_sf\,d\nu$. By the definition of $m$ and by $f(c)=m$, this equals $m\,\nu(s)=f(c)\int_sg\,d\mu$.

concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness of $s$ makes the image of $f$ an interval.
concepts.c:measurable-set: Measurability of $s$ lets the restricted integrals and $\nu$ be defined.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity on $s$ gives the intermediate value property.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability makes $\nu(s)$ finite and $f$ integrable for $\nu$.

source.note: mathlib passes to the a.e. version (ae_restrict_iff'), which uses withDensity, setIntegral_withDensity_eq_setIntegral_toReal_smul₀ and exists_eq_setAverage (IsPreconnected.intermediate_value on the sets f ≤ average and average ≤ f).

statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a [Grothendieck category](c:grothendieck-category) with a [generator](c:generator) $U$, and let $R=\mathrm{End}(U)$. Then $T=\mathrm{Hom}(U,-)\colon\mathcal A\to\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$ is fully faithful and has an exact left adjoint $S$. So $\mathcal A$ is equivalent to a [reflective subcategory](c:reflective-subcategory) of the [module category](c:module-category) $\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$, with exact reflector.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal A$ is a [Grothendieck category](c:grothendieck-category): abelian, with exact filtered colimits and a generator.
The object $U$ is a [generator](c:generator) of $\mathcal A$: the functor $\mathrm{Hom}(U,-)$ is faithful.

conclusion: The functor $T$ is fully faithful with an exact left adjoint, so $\mathcal A$ is a reflective subcategory of $\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$ up to equivalence.

proofs.name: Exact left adjoint of Hom(U,-)
proofs.slogan: Build the left adjoint of $\mathrm{Hom}(U,-)$, show that it is exact, and deduce that its counit is an isomorphism.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline of the proof of Popescu and Gabriel; the exactness of $S$ is the deep step and is cited. For $U=0$ the category is zero and the statement is trivial.

roles.why: Cocompleteness gives the left adjoint, and exact filtered colimits give the exactness of $S$.
A generator makes $T$ faithful and makes the counit an epimorphism.

steps.slogan: Define $T=\mathrm{Hom}(U,-)$ and show that it is faithful and preserves limits.
steps.detail: The group $T(X)$ is a right $R$-module by precomposition. $T$ preserves all limits, so it is left exact. It is faithful because $U$ is a [generator](c:generator): if $Tf=0$ then $f\circ u=0$ for every $u\colon U\to X$, so $f=0$.

steps.slogan: Construct the left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $S(M)=M\otimes_RU$ from the cocompleteness of $\mathcal A$.
steps.detail: A Grothendieck category has all colimits. Put $S(R)=U$, extend $S$ to free modules by coproducts and to all modules by cokernels. This gives $S\dashv T$ with $S(R)=U$ and $TS(R)=\mathrm{End}(U)=R$.

steps.slogan: Show that the counit $\varepsilon_X\colon STX\to X$ is an epimorphism.
steps.detail: The images of all maps $U\to X$ generate $X$, so $\bigoplus_{u\colon U\to X}U\to X$ is an epimorphism. This map factors through $\varepsilon_X$, so $\varepsilon_X$ is an epimorphism.

steps.slogan: Show that $S$ is an [exact functor](c:exact-functor).
steps.detail: This is the heart of the proof of Popescu and Gabriel. $S$ is right exact as a left adjoint, and a flatness test reduces exactness to the monomorphisms $S(I)\to S(R)=U$ for right ideals $I$. That step uses exact filtered colimits and the generator; it is cited, not reproduced.

steps.slogan: Deduce that every counit $\varepsilon_X$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: With $S$ exact and $T$ faithful, the cited proof shows that $\varepsilon_X\colon STX\to X$ is an isomorphism for every $X$. This is equivalent to $T$ being fully faithful.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\mathcal A$ is a reflective subcategory of $\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$ with exact reflector.
steps.detail: A fully faithful right adjoint identifies $\mathcal A$ with its essential image in $\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$. This image is a reflective subcategory with reflector $S$, and $S$ is exact.

concepts.c:grothendieck-category: Exact filtered colimits and a generator are the two properties used.
concepts.c:generator: The generator $U$ makes $T$ faithful and the counit an epimorphism.
concepts.c:reflective-subcategory: The conclusion presents $\mathcal A$ as the image of a fully faithful right adjoint.
concepts.c:module-category: The category $\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$ is the ambient category of the embedding.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The left adjoint $S$ gives the counit and the reflector.
concepts.c:exact-functor: Exactness of $S$ is the deep step of the proof.

source.ref: N. Popescu and P. Gabriel, Caracterisation des categories abeliennes avec generateurs et limites inductives exactes, Comptes Rendus Acad. Sci. Paris 258 (1964), 4188-4190; textbook proof: B. Stenstrom, Rings of Quotients, Springer, 1975, Theorem X.4.1
source.note: The outline follows Stenstrom, chapter X, section 4; the exactness of S is proved there.

statement: Let $X$ be a [Banach space](c:banach-space) with closed [unit ball](c:unit-ball) $B$, and let $B''$ be the unit ball of its [bidual](c:bidual) $X''$. The canonical embedding $J\colon X\to X''$ maps $B$ onto a subset of $B''$ that is dense for the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology).

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), real or complex, with closed [unit ball](c:unit-ball) $B$.

conclusion: Every point of $B''$ is a weak-star limit of a net in $J(B)$.

proofs.name: Hahn-Banach separation
proofs.slogan: Separate a point of $B''$ from the weak-star closure of $J(B)$ by an element of $X'$, and contradict the norm bound.
proofs.scope: Real and complex scalars; the complex case uses real parts. The proof does not use completeness of $X$.

roles.why: $X$ supplies the norm, the dual $X'$, the bidual and the ball $B$; completeness is not needed.

steps.slogan: Place $J(B)$ in the weak-star closed ball $B''$.
steps.detail: For $x\in B$ and $\varphi\in X'$, $|Jx(\varphi)|=|\varphi(x)|\le\|\varphi\|$, so $\|Jx\|\le1$ and $J(B)\subseteq B''$. The ball $B''=\bigcap_{\|\varphi\|\le1}\{z:|z(\varphi)|\le1\}$ is an intersection of weak-star closed sets, so it is weak-star closed.

steps.slogan: Let $K$ be the weak-star closure of $J(B)$ and note that it is convex and lies in $B''$.
steps.detail: The set $J(B)$ is a [convex set](c:convex-set), because $B$ is convex and $J$ is linear. The closure of a convex set in a topological vector space is convex. Closedness of $B''$ gives $K\subseteq B''$.

steps.slogan: Assume $z\in B''$ lies outside $K$ and separate $z$ from $K$ by a weak-star continuous functional.
steps.detail: The weak-star topology makes $X''$ locally convex, and its continuous linear functionals are the evaluations $w\mapsto w(\varphi)$ with $\varphi$ in the [dual space](c:dual-space) $X'$. Hahn-Banach separation gives $\varphi\in X'$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathrm{Re}\,z(\varphi)>c\ge\mathrm{Re}\,w(\varphi)$ for all $w\in K$.

steps.slogan: Bound $c$ from below by $\|\varphi\|$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,z(\varphi)$ from above by $\|\varphi\|$.
steps.detail: Take $w=Jx$ with $x\in B$: $\mathrm{Re}\,\varphi(x)\le c$. The supremum of $\mathrm{Re}\,\varphi(x)$ over $B$ is $\|\varphi\|$, so $\|\varphi\|\le c$. Also $\mathrm{Re}\,z(\varphi)\le|z(\varphi)|\le\|z\|\,\|\varphi\|\le\|\varphi\|$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two bounds to reach a contradiction and conclude that $K=B''$.
steps.detail: The bounds give $\|\varphi\|\le c<\mathrm{Re}\,z(\varphi)\le\|\varphi\|$, which is impossible. So no such $z$ exists, $B''\subseteq K$, and with $K\subseteq B''$ we get $K=B''$: $J(B)$ is weak-star dense in $B''$.

concepts.c:banach-space: The norm of $X$ defines the dual, the bidual and the unit balls.
concepts.c:unit-ball: The ball $B$ is the set whose image is shown to be dense in $B''$.
concepts.c:bidual: The bidual $X''$ is where the density statement lives.
concepts.c:weak-star-topology: Density is for this topology, whose functionals are evaluations at $X'$.

source.note: The standard proof by Hahn-Banach separation in the weak-star topology, as in Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, chapter V.

statement: Let $(P,\le)$ be a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order). Every [chain](c:chain) $C\subseteq P$ lies in a maximal chain: a chain $M\supseteq C$ that no larger chain of $P$ contains.

hypotheses.text: $(P,\le)$ is a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order).
The subset $C\subseteq P$ is a [chain](c:chain): any two elements of $C$ are comparable.

conclusion: There is a chain $M\supseteq C$ such that every chain containing $M$ equals $M$.

proofs.name: From Zorn's lemma
proofs.slogan: Apply Zorn's lemma to the chains that contain $C$, ordered by inclusion, and show that a maximal one is a maximal chain.
proofs.scope: The cases $P=\emptyset$ and $C=\emptyset$ are included: the family below is nonempty, and the empty subfamily has the upper bound $C$. The converse derivation of Zorn's lemma shows that the two principles are equivalent.

roles.why: The order $\le$ defines which subsets are chains.
The chain $C$ makes the family of chains containing $C$ nonempty.

steps.slogan: Collect all chains that contain $C$ into a family $\mathcal F$ ordered by inclusion.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal F=\{D\subseteq P: D\text{ is a chain and }C\subseteq D\}$ with the order $\subseteq$. This family is a [partial order](c:partial-order). It is nonempty because $C\in\mathcal F$.

steps.slogan: Show that the union of a chain of members of $\mathcal F$ belongs to $\mathcal F$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal K\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a nonempty chain under inclusion and $U=\bigcup\mathcal K$. Two elements of $U$ lie in members $D_1,D_2$ of $\mathcal K$, and one of them, say $D_2$, contains the other. So both elements lie in the chain $D_2$ and are comparable. Also $C\subseteq U$. For $\mathcal K=\emptyset$, the set $C$ is an upper bound.

steps.slogan: Apply Zorn's lemma to obtain a maximal member $M$ of $\mathcal F$.
steps.detail: By the previous step every chain in $(\mathcal F,\subseteq)$ has an upper bound in $\mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is nonempty. Zorn's lemma gives a [maximal element](c:maximal-element) $M$ of $\mathcal F$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ is a maximal chain of $P$.
steps.detail: The set $M$ is a chain and $C\subseteq M$. Let $D$ be a chain of $P$ with $M\subseteq D$. Then $C\subseteq D$, so $D\in\mathcal F$, and maximality of $M$ in $\mathcal F$ gives $D=M$.

concepts.c:partial-order: The order defines the chains and the inclusion order on the family $\mathcal F$.
concepts.c:chain: Chains are the objects collected, merged by union and maximized.
concepts.c:maximal-element: A maximal member of $\mathcal F$ is the maximal chain.

source.note: The standard derivation of the Hausdorff maximal principle from Zorn's lemma; see for example Kelley, General Topology, appendix.

statement: For nonzero rationals $a,b$, let $(a,b)_v=1$ if $ax^2+by^2=z^2$ has a nonzero solution over the [local field](c:local-field) $\mathbb Q_v$, and $-1$ otherwise. These [Hilbert symbols](c:hilbert-symbol) at the [places](c:place) $v$ of $\mathbb Q$ (the primes and $\infty$) equal $1$ for almost all $v$, and $\prod_v(a,b)_v=1$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $a$ and $b$ are nonzero rationals.

conclusion: $\prod_v(a,b)_v=1$, and only finitely many factors differ from $1$.

proofs.name: Local formulas and reciprocity
proofs.slogan: Compute the local symbols by explicit formulas, reduce to generators by bilinearity, and check the generator pairs with quadratic reciprocity.
proofs.scope: The proof covers $\mathbb Q$. For a general global field the product formula follows from global class field theory (the Artin reciprocity law).

roles.why: Nonzero $a,b$ have a valuation and a unit part at each prime, which the local formulas need.

steps.slogan: State the local formulas for $(a,b)_v$ at $\infty$, at $2$ and at odd primes.
steps.detail: Write $a=p^\alpha u$ and $b=p^\beta w$ with $p$-adic units $u,w$. For odd $p$, $(a,b)_p=(-1)^{\alpha\beta\varepsilon(p)}\bigl(\tfrac up\bigr)^\beta\bigl(\tfrac wp\bigr)^\alpha$ with the [Legendre symbol](c:legendre-symbol). For $p=2$, $(a,b)_2=(-1)^{\varepsilon(u)\varepsilon(w)+\alpha\omega(w)+\beta\omega(u)}$. Also $(a,b)_\infty=-1$ exactly when $a,b<0$. Here $\varepsilon(u)=\tfrac{u-1}2$ and $\omega(u)=\tfrac{u^2-1}8$ mod $2$. They follow from squares of units and Hensel's lemma (Serre, chapter III, theorem 1).

steps.slogan: Reduce the product formula to pairs of generators by bilinearity.
steps.detail: If $p$ is odd and $a,b$ are $p$-adic units, the formula gives $(a,b)_p=1$, so only finitely many factors differ from $1$. The symbol is bilinear in each variable, and $(a,a)_v=(a,-1)_v$ because $(a,-a)_v=1$. So it is enough to treat $(-1,-1)$ and the pairs of distinct elements of $\{-1,2\}\cup\{\text{odd primes}\}$.

steps.slogan: Check the pairs $(-1,-1)$, $(-1,2)$ and $(-1,l)$ for an odd prime $l$.
steps.detail: For $(-1,-1)$ the factors at $\infty$ and $2$ are both $-1$ and the others are $1$. For $(-1,2)$ all factors are $1$. For $(-1,l)$ the factors at $2$ and at $l$ are $(-1)^{\varepsilon(l)}$ and $\bigl(\tfrac{-1}l\bigr)$, which are equal by the first supplement of quadratic reciprocity.

steps.slogan: Check the pair $(2,l)$ for an odd prime $l$.
steps.detail: The factors at $2$ and at $l$ are $(-1)^{\omega(l)}$ and $\bigl(\tfrac2l\bigr)$, and all other factors are $1$. The two are equal by the second supplement of quadratic reciprocity, so their product is $1$.

steps.slogan: Check the pair $(l,l')$ of distinct odd primes.
steps.detail: The factors are $\bigl(\tfrac{l'}l\bigr)$ at $l$, $\bigl(\tfrac l{l'}\bigr)$ at $l'$ and $(-1)^{\varepsilon(l)\varepsilon(l')}$ at $2$; the others are $1$. Their product is $1$ by quadratic reciprocity, $\bigl(\tfrac l{l'}\bigr)\bigl(\tfrac{l'}l\bigr)=(-1)^{\varepsilon(l)\varepsilon(l')}$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the cases using bilinearity to get the product formula for all $a,b$.
steps.detail: Both sides of $\prod_v(a,b)_v=1$ are multiplicative in $a$ and in $b$. The group $\mathbb Q^\times$ is generated by $-1$, $2$ and the odd primes. So the generator cases give the formula for every pair $a,b\in\mathbb Q^\times$.

concepts.c:local-field: Each completion $\mathbb Q_v$ is a local field where the symbol is defined.
concepts.c:hilbert-symbol: The product of these local symbols is the object of the theorem.
concepts.c:place: The product runs over all places, the primes and $\infty$.
concepts.c:legendre-symbol: At odd primes the local symbol is a power of a Legendre symbol.

source.note: The proof of Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, chapter III, theorem 3, with the local formulas of theorem 1 of the same chapter.

statement: Let $X$ be a nonempty [H-space](c:h-space) with continuous product $\mu$ whose left and right translations are [weak homotopy equivalences](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence). The Hopf construction $H(\mu)\colon X*X\to\Sigma X$, $[x,t,y]\mapsto[\mu(x,y),t]$, from the join to the [suspension](c:suspension) is well defined, and its homotopy fibre over every point is weakly equivalent to $X$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a nonempty [H-space](c:h-space) with continuous product $\mu\colon X\times X\to X$.
For every $a\in X$, the maps $x\mapsto\mu(a,x)$ and $x\mapsto\mu(x,a)$ are [weak homotopy equivalences](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence).

conclusion: The map $H(\mu)$ is well defined and continuous, and its homotopy fibre over each point of $\Sigma X$ is weakly equivalent to $X$.

proofs.name: Homotopy pushouts and descent
proofs.slogan: Write $H(\mu)$ as a map of homotopy pushouts whose squares are homotopy pullbacks, and read the fibre from descent.
proofs.scope: The grouplike case, in the form with both translations equivalences; it includes $X=S^0,S^1,S^3,S^7$, where it gives the Hopf fibrations. The fibre is the homotopy fibre, not a strict fibre.

roles.why: The continuous product defines $H(\mu)$ and the diagram map.
Translations being equivalences makes both shear maps weak equivalences, so both squares are homotopy pullbacks.

steps.slogan: Check that the formula respects the identifications of the join and the suspension.
steps.detail: In $X*X=X\times[0,1]\times X/\!\sim$ the points $(x,0,y)$ do not depend on $y$ and the points $(x,1,y)$ do not depend on $x$. In $\Sigma X$ the ends $t=0$ and $t=1$ collapse to two points. The value $[\mu(x,y),t]$ respects both, so $H(\mu)$ is a well defined continuous map.

steps.slogan: Present the join and the suspension as [homotopy pushouts](c:homotopy-pushout) and $H(\mu)$ as a map between them.
steps.detail: The join is the double mapping cylinder of $X\xleftarrow{p_1}X\times X\xrightarrow{p_2}X$, and $\Sigma X$ is that of $*\leftarrow X\to*$. The map $H(\mu)$ is induced by the map of diagrams $(X\to*,\ \mu,\ X\to*)$.

steps.slogan: Show that both squares of the diagram map are homotopy pullbacks.
steps.detail: The left square is a homotopy pullback exactly when $(p_1,\mu)\colon X\times X\to X\times X$ is a weak equivalence. This shear map lies over the first factor, and on the fibre over $x$ it is the left translation by $x$. So it is a weak equivalence. The right square uses $(\mu,p_2)$ and right translations.

steps.slogan: Apply descent for homotopy pushouts to identify the homotopy fibre over the cone point.
steps.detail: By Mather's cube theorem, a map of pushout diagrams with homotopy cartesian squares is cartesian at every vertex. So $X\to X*X$, the inclusion of the end $t=0$, is the homotopy pullback of a cone point $*\to\Sigma X$ along $H(\mu)$. The homotopy fibre over the cone point is $X$.

steps.slogan: Move from the cone point to an arbitrary point of $\Sigma X$.
steps.detail: Since $X\ne\emptyset$, $\Sigma X$ is path connected: the path $t\mapsto[x,t]$ joins the two cone points, and each $[x,t]$ lies on it. Homotopy fibres over points of one path component are weakly equivalent. So every homotopy fibre of $H(\mu)$ is weakly equivalent to $X$.

concepts.c:h-space: The product $\mu$ of the H-space defines the Hopf construction.
concepts.c:weak-homotopy-equivalence: Translations being weak equivalences make the shear maps weak equivalences.
concepts.c:suspension: The suspension $\Sigma X$ is the base of the fibre sequence.
concepts.c:homotopy-pushout: The join and the suspension are homotopy pushouts, so descent applies.

source.note: The descent argument for homotopy pushouts (Mather's cube theorem); the statement agrees with the grouplike case recorded in the nLab entry on the Hopf construction.

statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a [stable ∞-category](c:stable-infinity-category). The functor that sends a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) $X$ to its sequence of skeleta $\operatorname{colim}_{\Delta^{op}_{\le0}}X\to\operatorname{colim}_{\Delta^{op}_{\le1}}X\to\cdots$ is an equivalence from $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^{op},\mathcal C)$ to the ∞-category $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathbb N,\mathcal C)$ of sequences $C_0\to C_1\to\cdots$ in $\mathcal C$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal C$ is a [stable ∞-category](c:stable-infinity-category).

conclusion: The skeleton functor $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^{op},\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathbb N,\mathcal C)$ is an equivalence of ∞-categories.

proofs.name: Skeletal filtration and truncation
proofs.slogan: Send a simplicial object to its skeleta, identify the layers with shifted nondegenerate parts, and compare the truncated categories one level at a time.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline of Lurie's proof; the truncated comparison is the deep step and is cited. In an abelian category the layers recover the normalized chain complex of the classical Dold-Kan correspondence.

roles.why: Stability makes cofibres into shifts and lets attaching data match on the two sides.

steps.slogan: Send a simplicial object to the sequence of its skeleta.
steps.detail: For $X\colon\Delta^{op}\to\mathcal C$ let $\mathrm{sk}_nX$ be the realization of the restriction of $X$ to $\Delta^{op}_{\le n}$. The inclusions $\Delta^{op}_{\le n-1}\subseteq\Delta^{op}_{\le n}$ give maps $\mathrm{sk}_{n-1}X\to\mathrm{sk}_nX$. This defines the functor $\Phi$ of the statement, built from the [skeleta](c:simplicial-skeleton).

steps.slogan: Identify the cofibre of $\mathrm{sk}_{n-1}X\to\mathrm{sk}_nX$ with a shift of the nondegenerate part.
steps.detail: Let $N_nX$ be the cofibre of the latching map $L_nX\to X_n$. In a stable ∞-category the [cofibre](c:cofiber) of $\mathrm{sk}_{n-1}X\to\mathrm{sk}_nX$ is $\Sigma^nN_nX$: the nondegenerate $n$-simplices contribute a copy of $\Delta^n/\partial\Delta^n\simeq S^n$.

steps.slogan: Match one-step extensions of truncated simplicial objects and truncated sequences.
steps.detail: Extending an $(n-1)$-truncated simplicial object to an $n$-truncated one amounts to choosing $N_n$ and an attaching map $\Sigma^{n-1}N_n\to\mathrm{sk}_{n-1}X$. Extending a sequence by one term amounts to the same data. So $\mathrm{Fun}(\Delta^{op}_{\le n},\mathcal C)\simeq\mathrm{Fun}([n],\mathcal C)$ by induction on $n$.

steps.slogan: Pass from the truncated equivalences to all of $\Delta^{op}$ and $\mathbb N$.
steps.detail: $\Delta^{op}$ is the union of the $\Delta^{op}_{\le n}$, and $\mathbb N$ is the union of the $[n]$. So both functor categories are limits of towers of truncated functor categories. The equivalences of the previous step commute with restriction, so they pass to the limit.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\Phi$ is an equivalence of ∞-categories.
steps.detail: The limit of the equivalences is an equivalence, and by construction it is $\Phi$. Its inverse realizes a sequence as a simplicial object by attaching one layer at a time.

concepts.c:stable-infinity-category: Stability turns cofibres into shifts and matches the attaching data.
concepts.c:simplicial-object: Simplicial objects are the source of the skeleton functor.
concepts.c:simplicial-skeleton: The skeleta give the filtration that the functor records.
concepts.c:cofiber: The layers of the filtration are cofibres of skeleton inclusions.

source.ref: J. Lurie, Higher Algebra, Theorem 1.2.4.1 (Dold-Kan correspondence), version of 2017
source.note: The outline follows section 1.2.4 of Higher Algebra: the skeletal filtration, its layers, and the comparison of truncated categories.

statement: Let $A$ be a unital associative algebra over a field $k$ of characteristic $0$, and let $\mathfrak{gl}(A)=\varinjlim\mathfrak{gl}_n(A)$, where $\mathfrak{gl}_n(A)$ is the [matrix algebra](c:matrix-algebra) $M_n(A)$ as a Lie algebra. Then $H_\bullet(\mathfrak{gl}(A))\cong\bigwedge\bigl(HC_{\bullet-1}(A)\bigr)$ as graded [Hopf algebras](c:hopf-algebra): the [Lie algebra homology](c:lie-algebra-homology) is the graded [exterior algebra](c:exterior-algebra) on the shifted [cyclic homology](c:cyclic-homology).

hypotheses.text: The field $k$ has characteristic $0$.
$A$ is a unital associative $k$-algebra.

conclusion: $H_n(\mathfrak{gl}(A);k)$ is the degree $n$ part of the free graded-commutative algebra on $HC_{\bullet-1}(A)$, and its primitive part is $HC_{n-1}(A)$.

proofs.name: Coinvariants and cyclic words
proofs.slogan: Reduce to primitive elements with the Hopf structure, compute coinvariants by invariant theory, and identify the result with Connes' cyclic complex.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for unital $A$ in characteristic $0$, as an outline of Loday and Quillen; the invariant theory step is cited. For $A=k$ it gives an exterior algebra on generators of degrees $1,3,5,\dots$.

roles.why: Characteristic $0$ gives the Milnor-Moore structure theorem, the semisimplicity of $\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)$-modules and the splitting of $\Lambda^p$.
The algebra $A$ supplies the matrices, the cyclic words and the cyclic homology.

steps.slogan: Give $H_\bullet(\mathfrak{gl}(A))$ a Hopf algebra structure and reduce to its primitive elements.
steps.detail: The block sum $\mathfrak{gl}_n(A)\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_m(A)\to\mathfrak{gl}_{n+m}(A)$ gives a product on $H_\bullet(\mathfrak{gl}(A))$, and the diagonal gives a coproduct. In characteristic $0$ the result is a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra), and by the Milnor-Moore theorem it is the free graded-commutative algebra on its primitive elements.

steps.slogan: Replace the Chevalley-Eilenberg complex by its $\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)$-coinvariants.
steps.detail: The reductive Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)$ acts semisimply on the complex $\Lambda^\bullet\mathfrak{gl}_n(A)$ and trivially on its homology. So $H_\bullet(\mathfrak{gl}_n(A))$ is the homology of the coinvariant complex $(\Lambda^\bullet\mathfrak{gl}_n(A))_{\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)}$.

steps.slogan: Compute the coinvariants by invariant theory in the stable range.
steps.detail: The first fundamental theorem of invariant theory shows that for $n\ge p$ the coinvariants of $\Lambda^p(M_n(k)\otimes A)$ are spanned by cyclic words in $A$. As $n\to\infty$ the complex becomes $\Lambda^\bullet\bigl(C^\lambda_{\bullet-1}(A)\bigr)$, where $C^\lambda_m(A)=A^{\otimes(m+1)}/(1-t)$ is Connes' cyclic complex.

steps.slogan: Pass to homology with the Künneth theorem in characteristic $0$.
steps.detail: In characteristic $0$ the functor $\Lambda^p$ is a direct summand of the $p$-th tensor power, so homology commutes with it. The homology of Connes' complex is [cyclic homology](c:cyclic-homology) $HC_\bullet(A)$. So $H_\bullet(\mathfrak{gl}(A))\cong\Lambda^\bullet(HC_{\bullet-1}(A))$.

steps.slogan: Identify the primitive part with $HC_{\bullet-1}(A)$ and match the Hopf structures.
steps.detail: The generators $HC_{n-1}(A)$ in degree $n$ are the primitive elements of the first step, because the product and coproduct of the stable complex are the block sum and the diagonal. So the isomorphism respects the [exterior algebra](c:exterior-algebra) and Hopf structures, and the primitive part of $H_n$ is $HC_{n-1}(A)$.

concepts.c:matrix-algebra: The Lie algebras $\mathfrak{gl}_n(A)$ are built from matrix algebras over $A$.
concepts.c:hopf-algebra: The Hopf structure reduces the computation to primitive elements.
concepts.c:lie-algebra-homology: The homology of $\mathfrak{gl}(A)$ is the object computed.
concepts.c:exterior-algebra: The answer is a graded exterior algebra on shifted cyclic homology.
concepts.c:cyclic-homology: Cyclic homology of $A$ is the homology of Connes' cyclic complex.

source.ref: J.-L. Loday and D. Quillen, Cyclic homology and the Lie algebra homology of matrices, Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici 59 (1984), 565-591
source.note: The outline follows Loday and Quillen; Tsygan proved the theorem independently in 1983.

statement: Let $B$ be a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) and $w(h)=\sup\{|B_t-B_s|:s,t\in[0,1],\ |t-s|\le h\}$ its [modulus of continuity](c:modulus-of-continuity). Almost surely, $\lim_{h\downarrow0}w(h)/\sqrt{2h\log(1/h)}=1$.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion): continuous paths, $B_0=0$, and [independent increments](c:independent-increments) with $B_t-B_s\sim N(0,t-s)$, a [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution).

proofs.name: Union bounds at geometric scales
proofs.slogan: Bound the increments above and below at the scales $\theta^k$ with Gaussian tails and Borel-Cantelli, then let $\theta\to1$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $B$ on $[0,1]$, with $\varphi(h)=\sqrt{2h\log(1/h)}$. The path $B$ is extended to $[0,\infty)$ so that grid points near $1$ make sense.

roles.why: Gaussian increments give the tail bounds, independence gives the lower bound, and continuity of paths makes $w$ a supremum over the grid.

steps.slogan: Record the Gaussian tail bounds and the reflection bound.
steps.detail: For $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $a>0$, $\frac a{1+a^2}\frac{e^{-a^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\le P(Z>a)\le\frac12e^{-a^2/2}$. The reflection principle gives $P(\max_{u\le T}|B_u|>x)\le2e^{-x^2/(2T)}$ for $x,T>0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the chance of a large increment on a fine grid at scale $h_k=\theta^k$.
steps.detail: Fix $\theta,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, put $\eta_k=\varepsilon^2h_k/3$ and $G_k=\eta_k\mathbb Z\cap[0,1)$. For $g\in G_k$ the tail bounds give $P\bigl(\max_{u\le(1+\varepsilon^2/3)h_k}|B_{g+u}-B_g|>(1+\varepsilon)\varphi(h_k)\bigr)\le2h_k^{1+\delta}$ with $\delta>\varepsilon$, and $P\bigl(\max_{u\le\eta_k}|B_{g+u}-B_g|>\varepsilon\varphi(h_k)\bigr)\le2h_k^3$. Since $|G_k|\le6/(\varepsilon^2h_k)$, the union bounds are summable over $k$, and Borel-Cantelli leaves finitely many bad $k$.

steps.slogan: Split each pair $s<t$ into grid pieces to get the upper bound.
steps.detail: Take $k$ so large that $h_k<1/e$ and no bad event occurs at any scale $j\ge k$. Let $h_{j+1}<t-s\le h_j$ and let $s',t'\in G_j$ lie just below $s,t$. Then $|B_t-B_s|\le|B_s-B_{s'}|+|B_{t'}-B_{s'}|+|B_t-B_{t'}|\le(1+3\varepsilon)\varphi(h_j)$, because $0\le t'-s'\le h_j+\eta_j$. For $h\in(h_{k+1},h_k]$ this gives $w(h)\le(1+3\varepsilon)\varphi(h_k)\le(1+3\varepsilon)\theta^{-1/2}\varphi(h)$, since $\varphi(h_{k+1})\ge\sqrt\theta\,\varphi(h_k)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the largest of $\lfloor1/h_k\rfloor$ independent increments from below.
steps.detail: The increments $B_{(j+1)h_k}-B_{jh_k}$ are independent $N(0,h_k)$. Each exceeds $(1-\varepsilon)\varphi(h_k)$ in absolute value with probability at least $c\,h_k^{(1-\varepsilon)^2}/\sqrt{\log(1/h_k)}$. So none does with probability at most $\exp(-c'h_k^{-\varepsilon(2-\varepsilon)}/\sqrt k)$, which is summable. By Borel-Cantelli and monotonicity of $w$, $w(h)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt\theta\,\varphi(h)$ for small $h$.

steps.slogan: Intersect countably many events and let $\theta\to1$ and $\varepsilon\to0$.
steps.detail: Almost surely, for all rational $\theta,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt\theta\le\liminf w/\varphi\le\limsup w/\varphi\le(1+3\varepsilon)/\sqrt\theta$. Letting $\theta\to1$ and $\varepsilon\to0$ gives the limit $1$.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: Brownian motion supplies the increments whose size is measured.
concepts.c:modulus-of-continuity: The modulus $w(h)$ is the quantity whose exact size is found.
concepts.c:independent-increments: Independence of disjoint increments gives the lower bound.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: Gaussian tails give the probability bounds at each scale.

source.note: Lévy's theorem (1937), proved here by union bounds at geometric scales; Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion, theorem 1.14, give a proof through Lévy's construction.

statement: Let $f(x,t)$ be a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) near $0$ in $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$ with $\partial_t^jf(0,0)=0$ for $j<k$ and $\partial_t^kf(0,0)\ne0$. Then near $0$, $f=c\cdot\bigl(t^k+\sum_{j<k}a_j(x)t^j\bigr)$ with $c$ smooth and $c(0,0)\ne0$, and $a_j$ smooth with $a_j(0)=0$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$, real or complex valued, is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) near $0\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$.
$\partial_t^jf(0,0)=0$ for $j<k$ and $\partial_t^kf(0,0)\ne0$.

proofs.name: Division and unit
proofs.slogan: Divide $t^k$ by $f$ with the Malgrange-Mather division theorem, then show that the quotient is a unit and the remainder vanishes at $x=0$.
proofs.scope: The preparation form for [germs](c:germ) of smooth functions at $0$. The division theorem of Mather is the cited ingredient, and its analytic analogue is the Weierstrass preparation theorem.

roles.why: Smoothness is the regularity class in which the division theorem holds.
Order $k$ in $t$ is the hypothesis of the division theorem and gives the unit $u$ in $f(t,0)=t^ku(t)$.

steps.slogan: Divide $t^k$ by $f$ with the Malgrange-Mather division theorem.
steps.detail: For $f$ as above, every smooth $g$ near $0$ is $g=qf+r$ with $q$ smooth and $r=\sum_{j<k}r_j(x)t^j$ with smooth $r_j$. Its long analytic proof is cited (Mather 1968; Hörmander, ALPDO I, section 7.5). Take $g=t^k$ to get $t^k=qf+r$.

steps.slogan: Factor $t^k$ out of $f(t,0)$.
steps.detail: Taylor's formula with integral remainder in $t$ gives $f(t,0)=t^ku(t)$ with $u$ smooth and $u(0)=\partial_t^kf(0,0)/k!\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Restrict the division identity to $x=0$ to show that $r(\cdot,0)=0$.
steps.detail: At $x=0$ the identity reads $t^k=q(t,0)\,t^ku(t)+r(t,0)$. So $r(t,0)=t^k(1-q(t,0)u(t))$ is a polynomial of degree less than $k$ that vanishes to order $k$ at $t=0$. Hence $r(t,0)=0$, that is, $r_j(0)=0$ for all $j$.

steps.slogan: Show that $q(0,0)\ne0$, so that $q$ is invertible near the origin.
steps.detail: Since $r(t,0)=0$, we have $t^k=q(t,0)\,t^ku(t)$. Dividing by $t^k$ for $t\ne0$ gives $q(t,0)u(t)=1$, so $q(0,0)u(0)=1$. Hence $q$ has no zero near $0$ and $1/q$ is smooth there.

steps.slogan: Write $f=q^{-1}(t^k-r)$ to obtain the preparation form.
steps.detail: From $t^k=qf+r$ we get $f=q^{-1}(t^k-r)$. Take $c=q^{-1}$ and $a_j=-r_j$. Then $c(0,0)\ne0$ and $a_j(0)=0$.

concepts.c:smooth-function: The division theorem and the factor $c$ live in the class of smooth functions.
concepts.c:germ: All statements concern germs at the origin, near which the identities hold.

source.ref: J. N. Mather, Stability of C-infinity mappings, I: The division theorem, Annals of Mathematics 87 (1968), 89-104; B. Malgrange, Ideals of Differentiable Functions, Oxford University Press, 1967
source.note: Mather's division theorem is the cited ingredient; Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, section 7.5, gives a textbook proof.

statement: For a nontrivial [finite subgroup of SU(2)](c:finite-subgroup-of-su-2) $G$, the quotient $\mathbb C^2/G$ is a [du Val singularity](c:du-val-singularity) whose [minimal resolution](c:minimal-resolution) has exceptional $(-2)$-curves in the pattern of an ADE [Dynkin diagram](c:dynkin-diagram) $\Delta_G$. The McKay graph of $G$ is the extended diagram of $\Delta_G$, and every ADE diagram arises from exactly one conjugacy class of $G$.

hypotheses.text: $G\ne1$ is a [finite subgroup of SU(2)](c:finite-subgroup-of-su-2).

conclusion: The exceptional curves form an ADE diagram $\Delta_G$, the McKay graph is its extended diagram, and $G\mapsto\Delta_G$ is a bijection from conjugacy classes to ADE types.

proofs.name: Classification, McKay graph and resolution
proofs.slogan: Classify the groups, show that the McKay graph is an extended ADE diagram, resolve the quotient, and match curves with representations.
proofs.scope: The whole correspondence, as an outline of the geometric McKay correspondence of Gonzalez-Sprinberg and Verdier. The steps on the classification and the McKay graph are classical (Klein, McKay).

roles.why: The group $G$ fixes the list of cases, the McKay graph and the quotient singularity.

steps.slogan: List the nontrivial finite subgroups of SU(2) up to conjugacy.
steps.detail: The double cover $SU(2)\to SO(3)$ and the classification of finite subgroups of $SO(3)$ give the cyclic groups $C_{n+1}$, the binary dihedral groups of order $4(n-2)$, and the binary tetrahedral, octahedral and icosahedral groups of orders $24$, $48$ and $120$. Each type is one conjugacy class (Klein).

steps.slogan: Show that the McKay graph is connected and has spectral radius $2$.
steps.detail: Let $Q$ be the natural representation and $a_{ij}=\dim\mathrm{Hom}_G(\rho_i\otimes Q,\rho_j)$ for the [irreducible representations](c:irreducible-representation) $\rho_i$. Since $Q\cong Q^*$, the matrix $(a_{ij})$ is symmetric. The identity $\sum_ja_{ij}\chi_j(g)=\chi_Q(g)\chi_i(g)$ for [characters](c:character-of-a-representation) shows that its eigenvalues are the numbers $\chi_Q(g)\in[-2,2]$, and $(\dim\rho_i)$ is a positive eigenvector for $2$. The graph is connected because $Q$ is faithful. So the spectral radius is $2$ by Perron-Frobenius.

steps.slogan: Identify the connected graphs of spectral radius $2$ with the extended Dynkin diagrams.
steps.detail: Smith's classification says that such a graph is one of $\tilde A_n$, $\tilde D_n$, $\tilde E_6$, $\tilde E_7$, $\tilde E_8$. The dimension vector is the null vector of the extended Cartan matrix, so $|G|=\sum_i(\dim\rho_i)^2$ fixes the order for each type. Comparing with the list of groups gives a bijection between conjugacy classes and types.

steps.slogan: Resolve $\mathbb C^2/G$ and read the configuration of its exceptional curves.
steps.detail: By Klein, $\mathbb C[x,y]^G$ has three generators and one relation, so $\mathbb C^2/G$ is a surface $\{F=0\}\subset\mathbb C^3$ with an isolated singularity of type $A_n$, $D_n$, $E_6$, $E_7$ or $E_8$. Its minimal resolution has exceptional curves $\mathbb P^1$ of self-intersection $-2$ that meet along the Dynkin diagram of the same type (Du Val).

steps.slogan: Match the exceptional curves with the nontrivial irreducible representations.
steps.detail: On the minimal resolution, each nontrivial $\rho_i$ gives a vector bundle $\mathcal R_i$ with $c_1(\mathcal R_i)\cdot E_j=\delta_{ij}$ (Gonzalez-Sprinberg and Verdier). So the curves $E_j$ correspond to the nontrivial vertices, and their intersection matrix is $-(2I-A')$ with $A'$ the McKay matrix without the trivial vertex. Thus $\Delta_G$ is the McKay graph minus the trivial vertex.

concepts.c:finite-subgroup-of-su-2: The group $G$ is the input of the whole correspondence.
concepts.c:du-val-singularity: The quotient $\mathbb C^2/G$ is a du Val singularity of ADE type.
concepts.c:minimal-resolution: Its exceptional curves carry the Dynkin diagram.
concepts.c:dynkin-diagram: The diagram records the exceptional curves and the McKay graph.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducible representations are the vertices of the McKay graph.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: Characters give the eigenvectors of the McKay matrix.

source.ref: G. Gonzalez-Sprinberg and J.-L. Verdier, Construction geometrique de la correspondance de McKay, Annales scientifiques de l'Ecole Normale Superieure, serie 4, 16 (1983), 409-449
source.note: The outline combines McKay (1980) for the graph, Klein and Du Val for the singularity, and Gonzalez-Sprinberg and Verdier for the matching; Reid, La correspondance de McKay (Seminaire Bourbaki 867), is a survey.
